sidney-kelly: His Police Gazette entry reads: 'Illicit drug trader. Drives his own motor car, and dresses well. Associates with criminals and prostitutes.'
Cocaine bought from a chemist for £1 could be retailed at £62 on the street. Kelly stood five foot three and carried a razor.
In 1928 he razor-slashed a woman named Betty Carslake at her home. His associate took the fall.
After prison he pioneered illegal baccarat in Sydney, earning roughly £1,000 a night during the wartime gambling boom.
He died of heart disease at forty-eight in his Centennial Park mansion. A hidden fortune of up to £100,000 was rumoured but never found.
Kelly associated with Kate Leigh, Tilly Devine, Nellie Cameron, and Melbourne gangster Squizzy Taylor. He was everyone's friend and nobody's.
d-ligores: Daniel Ligores was a Filipino showman turned Salvation Army cook, living at 110 Palmer Street, Darlinghurst — a street that would become the centre of Sydney's brothel trade.
His wife Gertrude had joined a Surry Hills free love cult at 62 Regent Street. The things that brought people to this part of Sydney rarely made the papers.
The Crown described him as 'a half-caste Chinese, born in Hong Kong.' Genealogical records say he was Filipino. The court didn't ask him.
Palmer Street, where Ligores lived, ran between Darlinghurst and Woolloomooloo. Filipino sailors, Chinese migrants, evangelical cults — all compressed into the same few blocks of terraces.
At trial he said: 'At Holt's Place I went mad.' The jury recommended mercy. He received a death sentence.
The Salvation Army kitchen where he cooked was on Kent Street in Surry Hills. The mission his wife joined was a fifteen-minute walk away.
edna-edgar: Photographed the day after Boxing Day, 1926. The holiday arrests filled the station — alcohol, arguments, the usual wreckage of celebration.
In two months the Pistol Licensing Act would pass, and the men who carried guns would switch to razors. Everything was about to change.
The 'A' suffix on her catalog number suggests a companion photograph — a second angle, or a second charge on the same night.
December 1926 fell in the brief window between the cocaine boom and the razor wars. The inner city was already a different country from the suburbs.
Women arrested at Central Station were commonly charged with vagrancy — a word that covered everything from homelessness to prostitution to simply lacking visible means of support.
Darlinghurst, Surry Hills, Woolloomooloo — an estimated five thousand drug addicts lived within a few square miles of this police station.
v-lowe: Valerie Lowe was nineteen. She and Joseph Messenger, eighteen, had broken into an army warehouse and stolen boots and overcoats worth £29.
Their Police Gazette entry describes Messenger as someone who 'violently resists arrest; frequents wine saloons, billiard rooms, racecourses.' They were teenagers stealing to survive.
The army warehouse theft was opportunistic — surplus military stores from the war, poorly guarded, full of things people needed.
Later that year they were arrested for stealing a saddle and bridle from Rosebery Racecourse. In 1923, Lowe broke into a house in Enfield and stole £40 in money and jewellery.
The archive photographs of the two have been described as 'an unexpectedly tender view' of a young pair. They are among the most reproduced images in the collection.

Real GDP had fallen nearly ten percent since 1914. Unemployment floated between six and eleven percent through the twenties. Lowe and Messenger were not organised criminals. They were young and broke.
d-poole: The L.B. on the charge sheet means licensed premises. Since 1916, every pub in Sydney closed at six o'clock sharp.
Men drank standing five deep at the bar, no seats allowed, sawdust on the floor. What happened after six happened somewhere else, and the law followed.
The six o'clock closing law was supposed to curb drunkenness. Instead it created the 'six o'clock swill' — workers finishing at five drinking as fast as they could before the taps shut off.
Pubs had been reduced to tiled rooms with no furniture. Patrons vomited where they stood rather than lose their place at the bar.
Kate Leigh's sly grog empire supplied illegal alcohol after six to thousands of customers across Surry Hills and Darlinghurst. The law created the market.
Licensed premises offences covered everything: selling after hours, harbouring criminals, allowing prostitutes on the premises, or simply running a pub that had become a headquarters.
f-schmidt: A German surname in 1923 Sydney still carried the weight of the war. German-Australians had been interned, their place names scrubbed from maps.
The inner city was emptying — those who could afford it moved to the outer suburbs. What remained were boarding houses, sly grog shops, and terrace houses where the rent was always late.
Surry Hills and East Sydney lost over ten percent of their population in the twenties. The people who stayed lived precariously close to real poverty.
Without a Drug Bureau or Licensed Premises prefix, Schmidt's plain catalog number suggests a general charge — theft, assault, fraud, or receiving stolen goods.
Returned soldiers from the war filled the inner-city boarding houses. Anti-German sentiment was personal for many of them. A name could be enough.

The terrace houses left behind by the suburban exodus were gradually filled by brothels, sly grog shops, SP betting rooms, and the growing class of people the newspapers called professional criminals.
ah-chong: The D on his file means Drug Bureau. Opium cost £1 per tin in China and sold for £10 in Sydney. The ships that carried the trade docked half a mile from this room.
Under the White Australia Policy, Chinese residents faced systematic surveillance. Drug laws were written with their names already in the margins.
The Dangerous Drugs Act had just introduced prison sentences for possession. Ah Chong's photograph was taken in the first year of that new regime.

Chinese Australians in 1920s Sydney were concentrated around Wexford Street and the Haymarket. The papers ran stories about opium dens. The prosecution numbers told a different story — just thirty-four cocaine offenders in all of New South Wales in 1929.
General Order 956 of the Department of Trade and Customs specifically referred to 'illegal possession of opium by Chinese or others.' The Chinese came first in the sentence.
'Ah' was a common Cantonese prefix, sometimes adopted as a westernised given name. The records used whatever version of your name was easiest for the clerk.
s-j-hay: Catalog number 167 — one of the earliest photographs in George Howard's project. Howard had only been the police photographer for two years.
He composed these like portraits. Careful lighting. No restraints. People standing however they chose. It was a small thing and it changed everything about what survived.
Howard joined the NSW Police in 1910 and became the official photographer for the fingerprint system in June 1920. He was noted for his 'artistic proclivities.'
His photographs were published in The Australasian Photo-Review. They were unlike police photographs anywhere else in the world.
The subjects were men and women recently plucked from the street, often still animated by the dramas surrounding their arrest. Howard let them compose themselves.
The archive was rescued in 1990 from a flooded warehouse in Lidcombe. Most of the original documentation explaining charges had been lost.
may-russel: January 1922. The women photographed here were allowed to hold their handbags, their papers, their cigarettes. They composed themselves as they liked.
The Vagrancy Act was the charge sheet's favourite word for women. It could mean almost anything. It usually meant the same thing.
The law made it illegal for men to live off earnings from sex work, but not for women to do the work itself. The distinction created an economy and then policed the people inside it.
Women like Ettie Sultana, a contemporary, accumulated convictions for prostitution, theft, drunkenness, swearing, and vagrancy. The categories blurred together on the charge sheets.
The 'Specials' photographs of women from this era are striking because of what they're allowed to be — composed, self-possessed, looking at the camera on their own terms.
Seventy-five percent of prostitutes in inner Sydney were cocaine users by the mid-twenties. The drug economy and the sex economy were the same economy.
e-falleni: Eugenia Falleni lived as Harry Crawford for over twenty years — working in factories, hotels, laundries. Married twice. No one knew.
At the preliminary hearing, the defendant appeared in men's clothes. At the trial in Darlinghurst, in women's. The press called it the most sensational case in Australian history.
Born in Italy, eldest of twenty-two children. As a teenager she dressed in men's clothes to work in brickyards and stables in New Zealand.
Crawford married Annie Birkett, a widow, in February 1913 at the Methodist Parsonage in Balmain South. They lived together for four years.
New South Wales had no laws governing gender identity in 1920. Falleni's identity was treated as a crime — 'sex fraud' — equal to or greater than the charge of murder.
Released after eleven years at Long Bay. Took the name Jean Ford. Ran a boarding house in Paddington. Struck by a car on Oxford Street in 1938. Buried under Anglican rites at Rookwood.
Upon arrest, Crawford asked to be held in the women's cells. The public galleries at the Darlinghurst courthouse were packed for every day of the trial.
g-lowe: D10 — among the first photographs processed through the new Drug Bureau. The Dangerous Drugs Act had made possession a prison offence for the first time that year.
By September 1928, Darlinghurst had earned the name Razorhurst. Five hundred slashings in three years, and cocaine was the currency underneath all of it.
Kate Leigh, the 'Snow Queen,' ran the largest cocaine supply network in Sydney from her base in Surry Hills. Phil Jeffs dealt from the 50-50 Club in Darlinghurst.
The Drug Bureau was staffed by Sergeants Wickham and Thompson, who targeted street-level dealers. The suppliers were harder to reach.
1928 was the first full year of the new drug enforcement regime. The law had changed. The trade hadn't.
Cocaine distribution was the economic engine of the razor gang violence. The slashings were territorial — not random, not personal. Business.
n-mcquade-l-stanley: Photographed together as suspected persons. The consorting clause had just passed — it made your friendships a crime if police decided you were the wrong kind of people.
It was 1930. Unemployment had reached twenty-one percent. The line between poverty and criminality was a distinction the law made and the streets did not.
In 1930, police arrested fifty-four men and sixty-two women for consorting. Sixty-eight were sentenced to prison. The following year the numbers doubled.

The Vagrancy Amendment Act 1929 was written specifically to combat the razor gangs. It criminalised 'habitually consorting with reputed thieves, or prostitutes, or persons convicted of having no visible lawful means of support.'
Being photographed as S.P. did not mean you had committed a crime. It meant the police considered your existence suspicious.
By 1932, unemployment would reach thirty-two percent. The Depression threw hundreds of thousands out of work and created a boom in illegal SP betting — the only economy still hiring.
patrick-riley: Convicted of making counterfeit coins and possessing a coining mould. Two years hard labour. Counterfeiting was considered an attack on the state itself.
The mould was the evidence that mattered. It meant he was manufacturing, not merely passing. A skilled trade, carried out in rented rooms with borrowed metal.
His alias was Matthew Edward Riley. The second name tells you the police had been looking for him under the first.
Counterfeiting required knowledge of metallurgy and access to materials. It was a craft. The courts treated it as treason against the currency.
His photograph appeared in the Police Gazette Photo Supplement of July 1926 — printed and distributed to officers across New South Wales so they could recognise him on the street.
Two years with hard labour meant stone-breaking, oakum-picking, or laundry work at Long Bay or Darlinghurst Gaol. The 'hard' was not a figure of speech.
v-stander: Vera Stander, alias Kelly. The S.P. on her file means suspected person — not charged with a crime, but placed on a watchlist for who she was seen with.
Her photograph was published in the Police Gazette so officers across New South Wales could recognise her on sight. The alias tells you she had been recognised before.
Aliases were common among the criminal class. Women frequently carried multiple identities — a different name for each neighbourhood, each encounter with the law.
Women designated S.P. were frequently suspected of involvement in prostitution, sly grog, or as associates of gang members. The charge was who you knew.
October 1926 — just months before the razor gang wars would explode across Darlinghurst and Surry Hills. The networks were already in place.
The Police Gazette photo supplements were a surveillance tool. Your face, printed in a government bulletin, distributed to every station in the state. The alias didn't help after that.
p-hume: June 1921. The six o'clock closing law had been running for five years, and sly grog was already an industry. The L.B. charge ties this to a pub or a hotel.
Returned soldiers, still carrying the war, filled the bars every afternoon. The law said stop drinking at six. Nobody stopped.
This is one of the earliest photographs in the archive. George Howard had assumed leadership of the photographic section only two months earlier, in April 1921.
Pubs were controlled by brewery monopolies — Tooth & Co dominated through tied houses. The spartan conditions encouraged rapid, desperate drinking.
The six o'clock closing law was designed to reduce drunkenness and send men home to their families. It produced the opposite — frantic drinking, then sly grog after dark.

Post-war demobilisation left many returned soldiers unemployed and damaged. The pubs were one of the few social institutions available to working-class men. The law shut the doors at six and offered nothing else.
e-park: 1929. The Royal Commission into police corruption was taking evidence. The razor gangs owned Darlinghurst. The Depression was three months away.
Sydney Hospital and St Vincent's treated the casualties. Surgeons learned to stitch razor wounds the way field medics had learned shrapnel — by volume.
The Crimes Amendment Act of 1930 would make possession of a cutthroat razor without good reason punishable by six months. The razors were that common.
Darlinghurst, Kings Cross, and Woolloomooloo were war zones in 1929. The violence was territorial — cocaine distribution routes, brothel boundaries, sly grog customers.
The Vagrancy Amendment Act passed that same year, its consorting clause written specifically for this moment. The law was trying to catch up to the streets.
Police arrested hundreds under the new consorting provisions. The courts were full. The gangs adapted. They always adapted faster than the legislation.
william-stanley-moore: His Police Gazette entry: 'Opium dealer. Operates with large quantities of faked opium and cocaine. A wharf labourer; associates with waterfront thieves and drug traders.'
Police raided four of his homes and found thirty-seven tins of opium. The waterfront gave him access to the ships. The faked product meant he cheated both the law and his customers.
In 1920, police found stolen bottles of morphia salts at his house in Kensington. By 1925, he had expanded to four addresses.
Moore's specialty was faked product — adulterated or counterfeit opium and cocaine. He was a manufacturer as much as a dealer.
European-manufactured cocaine, purchased freely in Asian ports, was smuggled into Sydney alongside opium by Chinese seamen. Moore's job as a wharf labourer put him at the point of arrival.

The same month Moore was arrested, NSW police uncovered a cocaine importing network for the first time — eighteen tins of opium, thirty-one bottles of cocaine, and a letter of introduction to a Chinese contact.
